lecture_context.lecture_title: Lecture 3: Full Cycle of a Deep Learning Project

unit.name: Benchmarks, drift, monitoring, and maintenance after deployment
unit.description: Closes the lifecycle by explaining reference performance, data/concept drift, operational monitoring, dashboard pruning, alarms, and model maintenance.
unit.summary: For model quality, the instructor introduces reference performance, often human-level performance, as an aspirational benchmark that helps diagnose whether a system is underperforming [ts=3263s]. After deployment, strong train/test performance is not enough because the world can change through data drift or concept drift: seasonal clothing, scarves, sunglasses, rain, geography, and user behavior can alter the distribution or the target mapping [ts=3310s]. Simple non-ML systems can sometimes be less susceptible to drift than high-capacity learned models because they tune fewer parameters and have fewer ways to overfit a narrow distribution [ts=3601s]. Production teams should gather privacy-respecting telemetry when possible, brainstorm possible failure modes, plot many metrics initially, prune uninformative dashboards, set alarms for abnormal ranges, and maintain the model by collecting new data and updating the system [ts=3735s].

key_points.text: Human-level performance can serve as a reference or aspirational benchmark for diagnosing model accuracy.
Data drift means the distribution of future inputs changes relative to the training set.
Concept drift means the input-output mapping changes relative to the training set.
Doing well on a test set is not the same as building a product that works in the real world.
Very simple non-ML systems may be less susceptible to drift because they tune fewer parameters than neural networks.
Production teams should use privacy-respecting telemetry, dashboards, pruning, and alarms to detect changing conditions.
Maintaining a deployed model means monitoring, collecting new data, and updating the system when new failures arise.

kp_catalog.name: Reference performance and human-level benchmark
kp_catalog.description: Reference performance, often human-level performance, is used as an aspirational or diagnostic benchmark for judging whether a model is underperforming.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: The lecture uses reference performance to connect evaluation to deployment readiness and to diagnose whether a model has room to improve [ts=3263s].

kp_catalog.name: Data drift and concept drift
kp_catalog.description: Data drift changes the distribution of future inputs, while concept drift changes the input-output mapping the model should learn.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: Drift is production-critical, but here it is one monitoring concern within the broader project lifecycle.

kp_catalog.name: Production monitoring and model maintenance
kp_catalog.description: Production ML teams monitor telemetry and dashboards, set alarms, collect new data, and update deployed systems when new failure modes appear.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: Maintenance is important production practice, but it supports the full lifecycle gateway rather than acting as a separate gate.
